newsitem.title: UK: HILLSBOROUGH SOCCER TRAGEDY RELIVED IN UK FILM.
newsitem.headline: HILLSBOROUGH SOCCER TRAGEDY RELIVED IN UK FILM.

text.p: Until April 15, 1989, Hillsborough was the above-average stadium of a once-mighty soccer team, used for English F.A. Cup semifinals simply because of its size.

But since that day, its name has been inextricably linked with the tragic deaths of 96 Liverpool football fans, crushed and smothered when too many supporters were allowed into an overcrowded stadium to watch their team play Nottingham Forest.
The events are to be relived on British television screens on Thursday in a two-hour drama/documentary made with the help of the bereaved families but in the teeth of police opposition.

The fans were unable to escape the crush because of "safety fences", designed to keep fans off the pitch and away from supporters of the opposing team, at a time when fighting and hooliganism was rife in the English game.
The game was played in Sheffield, northern England, following the tradition of choosing a neutral venue for finals matches.

Jimmy McGovern, the award-winning Liverpool-born writer of the drama, said the programme would show "senior officers in a state of frozen inaction", but he denied in an interview with the Guardian newspaper it was a simple police-bashing exercise.
"I wanted as well to be fair to the ordinary copper (police officer) on the ground who was let down by lack of leadership on the day," he said.
"The police were so bloody incompetent there was no need for us to exaggerate for dramatic effect," he added.
Controversy about police actions that day resurfaced in October when four officers were awarded compensation for the severe mental trauma they suffered.

Many of the relatives of the 96 who died at Hillsborough received no compensation, others got only modest sums. They questioned why police should be made a special case when they were only carrying out their normal duties.
Liverpool fans have felt maligned throughout.
In the days following the tragedy, newspapers reported -- falsely -- that drunken Liverpool fans had looted the corpses of supporters and urinated on police officers trying to save lives.

Those reports were rooted in the bad image of Liverpool fans after the Heysel stadium disaster in Brussels in 1985, when rampaging Liverpool fans caused the death of 39 spectators at a European Cup final against Italy's Juventus.

South Yorkshire police, responsible for policing the game in Sheffield, declined to comment before seeing the programme. A spokeswoman said the police had been unsuccessful in trying to obtain a preview copy.

But, according to various press reports, the police authority refused all cooperation with the film-makers and has said the programme ought not to be shown, because the events are still too close and the families will be upset.
"I think it is clear from the film who we reckon was to blame for the disaster," McGovern said. "We know what happened. If anyone thinks any of it is untruthful, then let them sue me."
